title: Philippians
tagline: A joyful letter from prison: Christ's humility, shared partnership, and contentment in every circumstance.
author: Paul
authorNote: The letter names Paul and Timothy (1:1), and almost all scholars accept it as Paul's. Some think chapter 3 (with its sudden warning, 3:2) or the thank-you note in 4:10-20 may have been separate pieces joined later, but there is no manuscript evidence for that and many scholars see one letter. The Christ hymn in 2:6-11 may be an earlier hymn that Paul quotes or his own composition.
audience: The church in Philippi, with its overseers and deacons
audienceNote: Philippi was the first European city where Paul founded a church (Acts 16), on his second journey. It was a Roman colony, proud of its Roman citizenship, with many retired soldiers. The church began with Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, and a jailer, and was one of the few that supported Paul financially (4:15-16).
setting: Paul in prison, probably in Rome, about AD 60 to 62 (debated)
settingNote: Paul writes from prison (1:7, 1:13-14), where he awaits a verdict that could mean death or release. Rome is the traditional place (the "imperial guard" in 1:13 and "Caesar's household" in 4:22 fit), but Ephesus (about AD 54 to 55) and Caesarea (about AD 58) have been suggested; the letter does not name the city. Epaphroditus has brought a gift from Philippi and has been seriously ill (2:25-30).
genreNote: A warm, personal letter, partly a thank-you note, partly a report of Paul's circumstances, and partly an appeal for unity. Joy and rejoicing run through it; the words "joy" and "rejoice" occur about sixteen times in four chapters.
bigIdea: Whatever happens, even prison and the threat of death, Christ is being proclaimed; the church should follow Christ's humility, stand united, and rejoice in him, finding contentment in every circumstance.
mapSummary: Philippi sits on the road across Macedonia from Neapolis toward Thessalonica; Paul writes from prison, traditionally in Rome.
